name: Umbelliferone
lead: Umbelliferone (7-hydroxycoumarin, C9H6O3) is a natural coumarin found in plants of the carrot family (Apiaceae) such as carrot, coriander and garden angelica, and in hydrangea and asafoetida.[1] It absorbs UV light strongly at about 300 to 325 nm and fluoresces blue, and is listed on Wikipedia as having been used as a sunscreen agent as well as an optical brightener, a dye-laser medium and a fluorescent indicator.[1]

For appearance, two uses are described. Its UV absorption is the basis for its listing as a sunscreen ingredient, which relates to protecting skin from photodamage and tanning.[1] A 2024 study reported that it lowered melanin production in cell tests and that a cream containing it lowered the melanin index and raised skin lightness after four weeks in a clinical test, leading the authors to describe it as a candidate skin-lightening ingredient for cosmetics.[10]
Most other published work concerns its use as a fluorescent probe, its metabolism, and animal and laboratory research on antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects.[2][3][4]

paras: Umbelliferone is a yellowish-white, odourless crystalline solid, slightly soluble in hot water and highly soluble in ethanol, and is biosynthesised from phenylalanine through cinnamic and coumaric acids.[1] It is the parent of many natural derivatives, including herniarin and the furanocoumarins such as psoralen.[1] Its glucuronides were described in 1955 and used for fluorimetric determination of beta-glucuronidase.[5]

Wikipedia lists carrot, coriander and garden angelica among its sources, along with mouse-ear hawkweed, bigleaf hydrangea (where it is called hydrangine), asafoetida and Justicia pectoralis; the name comes from the Umbelliferae family with umbrella-shaped flower clusters.[1] It is made in plants from phenylalanine through cinnamic and coumaric acid.[1] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes it as a plant defence compound and phytoalexin and reports it in Rutaceae such as grapefruit.[9]
In the laboratory it can be made by the Pechmann condensation of resorcinol, and related natural compounds include herniarin (the 7-O-methyl form), skimmin, and furanocoumarins such as psoralen.[1]

In animal and cell models, umbelliferone has been reported to protect against cyclophosphamide-induced liver toxicity in association with Nrf2 and PPAR-gamma up-regulation,[6] and coumarins in general have been reviewed as modulators of the Keap1/Nrf2 pathway.[4][7] Grokipedia and Wikipedia also note reports of antioxidant activity and inhibition of the enzyme 17-beta-HSD type 3 in vitro.[1] Coumarin extracts from Angelica roots showed analgesic and anti-inflammatory activity in rodents.[3] Coumarins have also been reported to reduce E. coli O157:H7 biofilm formation in the laboratory.[8]
Umbelliferone has also been examined as a building block in prodrug design, where phytophenols serve as carriers,[11] and in a 2025 animal study on diabetic muscle wasting.[12]

Wikipedia lists sunscreen use based on its UV absorption.[1] Its absorption in the UVB and short UVA range and its fluorescence are the properties cited; no efficacy or safety trial of umbelliferone in commercial sunscreens was located, and Wikipedia flags that some claims on its page are poorly referenced.[1]

A 2024 paper in Molecules by Kim and colleagues examined umbelliferone for melanin control. In lab tests it was not toxic to human skin cells or B16F10 melanoma cells, and it reduced melanin content and tyrosinase activity in a dose-dependent way, with lower tyrosinase mRNA.[10] A formulation containing it remained stable at different temperatures, and after four weeks of topical application in a clinical study the melanin index decreased and skin lightness (L*) increased relative to baseline.[10] The authors concluded it is a promising skin-lightening agent for cosmetics.[10] The study is a single report, and no larger or independent trial has been published.

One human study is available: the 2024 Molecules paper reported a four-week topical clinical test in which the melanin index fell and skin lightness rose from baseline.[10] No studies found of umbelliferone as a topical photoprotective sunscreen. Other related work on coumarins generally is laboratory or animal research.[7][9]

card.summary: Plant coumarin that absorbs UVB/short UVA and is listed as a sunscreen agent; actual evidence is lab chemistry and animal work.
card.note: No human studies as a sunscreen; Wikipedia flags weak sourcing on some uses.

quick.overview:
Umbelliferone is a natural coumarin found in carrots, coriander, angelica and hydrangea. It absorbs ultraviolet light and glows blue, which is why it appears as a sunscreen agent and a fluorescent dye.

Research on it is mostly laboratory and animal work on antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects.
quick.mechanism: The coumarin ring absorbs UV around 300 to 325 nm. In cell and animal studies it is reported to act on the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway.
quick.risks: No human safety or efficacy trials as a sunscreen were found. Its absorption shifts in alkaline conditions, and related furanocoumarins such as psoralen are distinct compounds.

chain: Absorbs UV light and lowers tyrosinase activity in cell tests
Less melanin production in cultured cells; lower melanin index in a 4-week topical study
angle.text: Umbelliferone is discussed as a cosmetic ingredient for skin brightening and as a UV-absorbing sunscreen component. The skin-lightening evidence consists of a 2024 laboratory and clinical study by one research group.
